LESSON 34 OF 106·Cryptography Essentials

Key Management: Generate, Store, Rotate, Revoke

Where cryptography meets operations: generating keys from real randomness, storing them away from the data, rotating on a schedule, and revoking before you are forced to.

Foundation14 min
Why this matters

Most organisations can deploy strong cryptography and still lose data because the keys are poorly managed. The algorithm is rarely the weak point; storage, rotation and revocation are.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Keys are generated with a good random source, then stored somewhere with tighter access than the data they protect.
  • Separate keys per purpose and per environment, so a test key can never be used against production data.
  • Rotation limits how much traffic or data a single key can expose, and rotation only helps if it actually happens.
  • Revocation says a key must never be used again, which requires something that checks rather than something that logs.
  • A key management system should record who used which key for what, because that is what an investigation needs.

The background

  • Keys were once kept in application configuration, which meant they appeared in source control and in every copy of the system.
  • Hardware security modules gave a place to keep keys that code could use but could not read.
  • Cloud secret managers made managed keys broadly available, but also created a central point of failure worth attacking.
  • Managed key management with automatic rotation became the default expectation, which makes manual key handling the outlier.

Real-world examples

  • A key committed to a source repository may still be live years later, and history makes deleting the file irrelevant.
  • One key reused across every environment means a single test-system compromise can affect production data.
  • A key that is rotated but never retired leaves the old one usable, so the rotation provides no benefit at all.

What to look for

  • Check whether keys appear in source control, build logs, container images or client-side code.
  • Confirm development, test and production use different keys.
  • Check whether retired keys are actually destroyed, and whether that is verified rather than assumed.
  • Check who can read keys, and whether that access is logged.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 — Key Management Recommendation

Reading the reference vocabulary for key lifecycle stages, owners and custodians, then applying it to classify the controls missing from your own inventory

Open NIST resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Store keys in a managed secret store or hardware module, never in application code or configuration files.
  • Use separate keys per environment and per purpose, and label them so misuse is obvious.
  • Automate rotation, and verify that old material is destroyed afterwards.
  • Give key access its own access reviews, since it is more sensitive than the data itself.
  • Scan source history and build artefacts for secrets, because removing them later does not remove them.
  • Rehearse revocation, since a key you cannot revoke is really a key you cannot rotate.
